title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |

    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068", "af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a", "c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf", "d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da", "8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854", "b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09", "ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1", "20965254e29104986e11939decd39549", "18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883", "0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d", "5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355", "fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6", "74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80") or SHA1 in~ ("95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068", "af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a", "c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf", "d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da", "8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854", "b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09", "ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1", "20965254e29104986e11939decd39549", "18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883", "0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d", "5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355", "fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6", "74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80") or MD5 in~ ("95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068", "af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a", "c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf", "d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da", "8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854", "b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09", "ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1", "20965254e29104986e11939decd39549", "18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883", "0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d", "5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355", "fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6", "74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068", "af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a", "c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf", "d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da", "8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854", "b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09", "ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1", "20965254e29104986e11939decd39549", "18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883", "0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d", "5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355", "fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6", "74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80") or SHA1 in~ ("95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068", "af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a", "c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf", "d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da", "8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854", "b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09", "ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1", "20965254e29104986e11939decd39549", "18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883", "0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d", "5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355", "fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6", "74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80") or MD5 in~ ("95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068", "af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a", "c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf", "d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da", "8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854", "b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09", "ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1", "20965254e29104986e11939decd39549", "18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883", "0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d", "5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355", "fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6", "74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068", "af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a", "c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf", "d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da", "8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854", "b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09", "ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1", "20965254e29104986e11939decd39549", "18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883", "0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d", "5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355", "fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6", "74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SprySOCKS (FishMonger/I-SOON) C2 beacon to hardcoded Vultr IPs 207.148.78.36 / 207.148.75.122 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the two hardcoded SprySOCKS infrastructure IPs ESET attributed to FishMonger: WIN_PLUS C&C 207.148.78.36 (TCP/UDP/WebSocket on 443/53/80) and delivery server 207.148.75.122. These are hard IOCs confirmed by multiple vendors, so any egress to them is high-fidelity regardless of the initiating binary (the WIN_DRV variant diverts C2 over a random TCP port, so do not pin on a fixed listening port). Rationale: Uses the two ESET-published hardcoded IPs (207.148.78.36 C&C and 207.148.75.122 delivery server), each confirmed by Security Affairs and gbhackers. Matching on exact IP rather than the broader shared Vultr /20 keeps FP near zero. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/fishmongers-arsenal-upgraded-sprysocks-windows/ • https://securityaffairs.com/193728/apt/china-linked-fishmonger-ports-sprysocks-to-windows-with-kernel-level-stealth-and-uefi-bootkit-hints.html • https://gbhackers.com/sprysocks-windows-backdoor-uses-kernel/
ATT&CKT1071 T1095 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A different, benign tenant workload legitimately rents the same recycled Vultr IP after the campaign infrastructure was torn down (Vultr IPs are reassigned)
  • Security researcher / sandbox detonation host in your environment deliberately contacting the IOC
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling or IOC-validation scanner probing the address
  • NAT/proxy egress IP making the source attribution ambiguous (confirm the real internal host)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal host and the InitiatingProcessFileName/SHA1 making the connection; pull the process tree and check whether the binary SHA1 matches the SprySOCKS hash list (UC2). 2) Contain: network-isolate the host, block 207.148.78.36, 207.148.75.122 and review the wider 207.148.64.0/20 Vultr range at the perimeter; preserve memory for the kernel-driver rootkit. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for unsigned/hidden kernel driver loads, hidden listening ports, EFI System Partition tampering (UC3), and any other host beaconing to the same /20.

| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession

| order by TimeGenerated desc

SprySOCKS WIN_DRV/WIN_PLUS backdoor binary by ESET SHA1 hash AIInstallation Medium
Detects execution, file write, or image load of any of the 11 SprySOCKS Windows binaries (WIN_DRV / WIN_PLUS variants and loaders) by their ESET-published SHA1 hashes. WIN_DRV ships a kernel driver that hides its own processes, files, registry keys and network connections, so on-host hash matching at write/load time is the most reliable surface before the rootkit engages. Rationale: All 11 SHA1 values are the ESET-published SprySOCKS sample hashes from the article IOC block, cross-checked against the ESET blog mirror and Security Affairs. Hash matching is exact and survives the rootkit's process/file hiding because it fires at write/load time. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/fishmongers-arsenal-upgraded-sprysocks-windows/ • https://www.esetngblog.com/post/fishmonger-s-arsenal-upgraded-sprysocks-for-windows • https://securityaffairs.com/193728/apt/china-linked-fishmonger-ports-sprysocks-to-windows-with-kernel-level-stealth-and-uefi-bootkit-hints.html
ATT&CKT1014 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AV/EDR quarantine copies or VirusTotal-uploaded sample handling on an analyst/sandbox host re-surfacing the same hash
  • Threat-intel platform storing the sample on disk during enrichment
  • Re-used hash from a generic packer producing a benign-file collision (extremely unlikely for SHA1, but verify file path/signer)
  • Purple-team or detection-validation exercise intentionally dropping the IOC
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the hit is on a production endpoint (not a sandbox/IR jump box); capture FolderPath, signer, and the InitiatingProcess that wrote/loaded it. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately, collect a memory image before the kernel driver can re-hide artifacts, and submit the binary for analysis. 3) Hunt: search the org for any of the other 10 hashes, for connections to the UC1 C2 IPs, for service installations and EFI/boot tampering (UC3), and scope FishMonger lateral movement to other government/high-value hosts.

SprySOCKS WIN_DRV BlackLotus-style Secure Boot downgrade / EFI bootkit (CVE-2023-24932) AIInstallation Low
Hunts for the UEFI bootkit component ESET reports as a 'limited indication' in some SprySOCKS attacks: a CVE-2023-24932 BlackLotus-style downgrade that writes a revoked/older boot manager (bootmgfw.efi/bootmgr.efi/bootx64.efi) onto the EFI System Partition. Flags .efi writes to boot paths by processes other than the Windows servicing stack — the EDR-blind firmware persistence this campaign may layer on top of the kernel rootkit. Rationale: Targets the article's CVE-2023-24932 UEFI bootkit lead by detecting the BlackLotus-style core action — writing a (revoked/downgraded) boot manager to the EFI System Partition — excluding the Windows servicing stack that legitimately updates these files. Confidence is Low because ESET itself frames the bootkit as a 'limited indication'. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/fishmongers-arsenal-upgraded-sprysocks-windows/ • https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/topic/how-to-manage-the-windows-boot-manager-revocations-for-secure-boot-changes-associated-with-cve-2023-24932-41a975df-beb2-40c1-99a3-b3ff139f832d • https://www.huntress.com/threat-library/vulnerabilities/cve-2023-24932
ATT&CKT1542.003 T1553.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Windows cumulative/feature update or KB5025885 Secure Boot servicing applying the boot manager (TrustedInstaller/TiWorker — filtered, but third-party servicing tools may not be)
  • OEM/IT imaging and BCD repair via bcdboot.exe / dism during provisioning
  • BitLocker recovery or bootrec /rebuildbcd troubleshooting by a sysadmin
  • Endpoint backup/restore agents touching the ESP
  • Dual-boot or Linux bootloader (e.g. shim/grub) installation writing .efi files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("bcdboot.exe","dism.exe","setuphost.exe","reagentc.exe") and not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Windows\WinSxS\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the writing process and its signer; confirm whether it is a sanctioned servicing/imaging tool and whether the dropped .efi is Microsoft-signed and current (compare hash/version against a known-good). 2) Contain: if non-servicing, isolate the host, verify Secure Boot state and DBX revocation status, and treat as firmware-level compromise — reimage may be insufficient; rebuild the ESP from trusted media. 3) Hunt: correlate the host with UC1 C2 beacons and UC2 SprySOCKS hashes, review for Memory Integrity/HVCI or BitLocker being disabled, unrecognized .efi files, BCD edits, and apply CVE-2023-24932 DBX revocations fleet-wide.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName endswith ".efi"
| where FileName in~ ("bootmgfw.efi","bootmgr.efi","bootx64.efi") or FolderPath has @"\EFI\" or FolderPath has "HarddiskVolume"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("TiWorker.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","poqexec.exe","MoUsoCoreWorker.exe","CompatTelRunner.exe","wuauclt.exe","setup.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".efi"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("bootmgfw.efi","bootmgr.efi","bootx64.efi") or TargetFilePath has @"\EFI\" or TargetFilePath has "HarddiskVolume"
| where ActingProcessName !has "TrustedInstaller.exe" and ActingProcessName !has "TiWorker.exe" and ActingProcessName !has "poqexec.exe" and ActingProcessName !has "CompatTelRunner.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, DvcAction, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA1
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Boot Manager EFI Write to EFI System Partition (CVE-2023-24932 Bootkit Downgrade)
id: 9d4a1f72-08be-4c63-bb15-7a2e6c0f9b31
description: Detects writes of bootmgfw.efi/bootmgr.efi/bootx64.efi to the EFI System Partition by a non-servicing process, consistent with a CVE-2023-24932 BlackLotus-style downgrade observed alongside SprySOCKS WIN_DRV.
references:
  - https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/fishmongers-arsenal-upgraded-sprysocks-windows/
  - https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/topic/how-to-manage-the-windows-boot-manager-revocations-for-secure-boot-changes-associated-with-cve-2023-24932-41a975df-beb2-40c1-99a3-b3ff139f832d
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/20
tags:
  - attack.t1542.003
  - attack.t1553.006
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\bootmgfw.efi'
      - '\bootmgr.efi'
      - '\bootx64.efi'
  filter_servicing:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\TrustedInstaller.exe'
      - '\TiWorker.exe'
      - '\poqexec.exe'
      - '\CompatTelRunner.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_servicing
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\bootmgfw.efi OR *\\bootmgr.efi OR *\\bootx64.efi OR *\\EFI\\* OR *\\bootmgfw.EFI OR *\\BOOTMGFW.EFI) -@Image:(*\\TrustedInstaller.exe OR *\\TiWorker.exe OR *\\poqexec.exe OR *\\CompatTelRunner.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\\(bootmgfw|bootmgr|bootx64)\.efi$/i
| NOT (ContextImageFileName=/\\(TrustedInstaller|TiWorker|poqexec|CompatTelRunner|wuauclt)\.exe$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name IN ("bootmgfw.efi","bootmgr.efi","bootx64.efi") OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\EFI\\*") AND Filesystem.file_name="*.efi" AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("TiWorker.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","poqexec.exe","MoUsoCoreWorker.exe","CompatTelRunner.exe","wuauclt.exe") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name IN ("bootmgfw.efi","bootmgr.efi","bootx64.efi") OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\EFI\\*") AND Filesystem.file_name="*.efi" AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("TiWorker.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","poqexec.exe","MoUsoCoreWorker.exe","CompatTelRunner.exe","wuauclt.exe") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2023-24932")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2023-24932")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("955BFC3DCC867256F9F46A606DEB0779FA3416D8", "44DC4A08C5EB0972C8E18B0E01284E06F09006BB", "AB87B29B6F79487C75CA08D102E79001E536F083", "6490B8E4AADE25A3EE2DA9A47F312DB2122470BC", "E7484C24B88A1A2407A8F09D734F9A993670285B", "621D1952839BE4B0A1B0E66E87BCE5062CA368ED", "2457EED2AB28E37741F10914EF929DAD2C8079D4", "D2C706B1EAF662BF0CE124B5032F73ED84BDA24A", "5F3B87CEF56683D9A9E19186E0FD0D8019B559C4", "C793CA31E3F6628B5C8986146953BF66232E9A30", "037DB2445F3D72388CB2CF8510563148E5A184BE") or SHA1 in~ ("955BFC3DCC867256F9F46A606DEB0779FA3416D8", "44DC4A08C5EB0972C8E18B0E01284E06F09006BB", "AB87B29B6F79487C75CA08D102E79001E536F083", "6490B8E4AADE25A3EE2DA9A47F312DB2122470BC", "E7484C24B88A1A2407A8F09D734F9A993670285B", "621D1952839BE4B0A1B0E66E87BCE5062CA368ED", "2457EED2AB28E37741F10914EF929DAD2C8079D4", "D2C706B1EAF662BF0CE124B5032F73ED84BDA24A", "5F3B87CEF56683D9A9E19186E0FD0D8019B559C4", "C793CA31E3F6628B5C8986146953BF66232E9A30", "037DB2445F3D72388CB2CF8510563148E5A184BE") or MD5 in~ ("955BFC3DCC867256F9F46A606DEB0779FA3416D8", "44DC4A08C5EB0972C8E18B0E01284E06F09006BB", "AB87B29B6F79487C75CA08D102E79001E536F083", "6490B8E4AADE25A3EE2DA9A47F312DB2122470BC", "E7484C24B88A1A2407A8F09D734F9A993670285B", "621D1952839BE4B0A1B0E66E87BCE5062CA368ED", "2457EED2AB28E37741F10914EF929DAD2C8079D4", "D2C706B1EAF662BF0CE124B5032F73ED84BDA24A", "5F3B87CEF56683D9A9E19186E0FD0D8019B559C4", "C793CA31E3F6628B5C8986146953BF66232E9A30", "037DB2445F3D72388CB2CF8510563148E5A184BE")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("955BFC3DCC867256F9F46A606DEB0779FA3416D8", "44DC4A08C5EB0972C8E18B0E01284E06F09006BB", "AB87B29B6F79487C75CA08D102E79001E536F083", "6490B8E4AADE25A3EE2DA9A47F312DB2122470BC", "E7484C24B88A1A2407A8F09D734F9A993670285B", "621D1952839BE4B0A1B0E66E87BCE5062CA368ED", "2457EED2AB28E37741F10914EF929DAD2C8079D4", "D2C706B1EAF662BF0CE124B5032F73ED84BDA24A", "5F3B87CEF56683D9A9E19186E0FD0D8019B559C4", "C793CA31E3F6628B5C8986146953BF66232E9A30", "037DB2445F3D72388CB2CF8510563148E5A184BE") or SHA1 in~ ("955BFC3DCC867256F9F46A606DEB0779FA3416D8", "44DC4A08C5EB0972C8E18B0E01284E06F09006BB", "AB87B29B6F79487C75CA08D102E79001E536F083", "6490B8E4AADE25A3EE2DA9A47F312DB2122470BC", "E7484C24B88A1A2407A8F09D734F9A993670285B", "621D1952839BE4B0A1B0E66E87BCE5062CA368ED", "2457EED2AB28E37741F10914EF929DAD2C8079D4", "D2C706B1EAF662BF0CE124B5032F73ED84BDA24A", "5F3B87CEF56683D9A9E19186E0FD0D8019B559C4", "C793CA31E3F6628B5C8986146953BF66232E9A30", "037DB2445F3D72388CB2CF8510563148E5A184BE") or MD5 in~ ("955BFC3DCC867256F9F46A606DEB0779FA3416D8", "44DC4A08C5EB0972C8E18B0E01284E06F09006BB", "AB87B29B6F79487C75CA08D102E79001E536F083", "6490B8E4AADE25A3EE2DA9A47F312DB2122470BC", "E7484C24B88A1A2407A8F09D734F9A993670285B", "621D1952839BE4B0A1B0E66E87BCE5062CA368ED", "2457EED2AB28E37741F10914EF929DAD2C8079D4", "D2C706B1EAF662BF0CE124B5032F73ED84BDA24A", "5F3B87CEF56683D9A9E19186E0FD0D8019B559C4", "C793CA31E3F6628B5C8986146953BF66232E9A30", "037DB2445F3D72388CB2CF8510563148E5A184BE")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["955BFC3DCC867256F9F46A606DEB0779FA3416D8", "44DC4A08C5EB0972C8E18B0E01284E06F09006BB", "AB87B29B6F79487C75CA08D102E79001E536F083", "6490B8E4AADE25A3EE2DA9A47F312DB2122470BC", "E7484C24B88A1A2407A8F09D734F9A993670285B", "621D1952839BE4B0A1B0E66E87BCE5062CA368ED", "2457EED2AB28E37741F10914EF929DAD2C8079D4", "D2C706B1EAF662BF0CE124B5032F73ED84BDA24A", "5F3B87CEF56683D9A9E19186E0FD0D8019B559C4", "C793CA31E3F6628B5C8986146953BF66232E9A30", "037DB2445F3D72388CB2CF8510563148E5A184BE"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Fake Microsoft account security-alert spear-phish delivering ZIP-with-LNK (APT37/ScarCruft) · [LLM] NarwhalRAT LNK-spawned batch downloader fetching payload + CAT file from APT37 C2 · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] NarwhalRAT scheduled-task persistence by exact task name (MicrosoftUserInterfacePicturesUpdateTackMachine) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] NarwhalRAT C2 to APT37 Korean relay domains/IPs · [LLM] NarwhalRAT pCloud dead-drop resolver secondary C2 from Python loader · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] NarwhalRAT 'naverwhale' staging directory under %APPDATA% · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Fake Microsoft account security-alert spear-phish delivering ZIP-with-LNK (APT37/ScarCruft) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound email impersonating a Microsoft Account security/OTP alert from a non-Microsoft sender domain that carries a ZIP attachment (the NarwhalRAT delivery vector observed by Genians). The article's lure is a fake 'abnormal OTP activity' notice whose attachment is a ZIP containing a malicious LNK rather than the promised HWP advisory. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact lure (fake MS account/OTP security alert) + the specific delivery shape (inbound ZIP attachment from a non-Microsoft sender domain). Sentinel left empty: this tenant's Sentinel schema has no native O365 email/attachment table (EmailEvents is Defender XDR only); detect via Defender AH instead. Cross-checked against: • https://www.genians.co.kr/en/blog/threat_intelligence/narwhalrat • https://gbhackers.com/apt37-hackers-use-narwhalrat-malware/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/powershell-and-python-loader-to-deploy-narwhalrat/
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1656
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate breach/credential-alert digests from third-party password managers or identity providers using 'security alert' subjects
  • Internal phishing-simulation campaigns spoofing Microsoft branding
  • Partner/vendor sending genuine .zip with 'security' in the subject (audit reports, SBOMs)
  • Marketing newsletters from security vendors with Microsoft in the display name
Suppression filter
| where AuthenticationDetails has_any ("spf:fail","dmarc:fail","compauth:fail","spf:softfail")
Response runbook
1) Triage: detonate/examine the ZIP in a sandbox — confirm it contains a .lnk (not the promised HWP). Check SPF/DKIM/DMARC alignment in AuthenticationDetails and whether SenderDisplayName spoofs Microsoft over a mismatched domain. 2) Contain: purge the message tenant-wide (soft-delete + block sender domain/IP), and check UrlClickEvents/DeviceFileEvents for any recipient who already extracted or ran the LNK. 3) Hunt: on any host that opened the attachment, pivot to UC2-UC6 — schtasks named MicrosoftUserInterfacePicturesUpdateTackMachine, %APPDATA%\naverwhale, and connections to daehoat.com / novel21.co.kr.
let LookbackDays = 14d;

| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where DeliveryAction in ("Delivered","DeliveredAsSpam")
| where SenderDisplayName has_any ("Microsoft","Microsoft Account","Account Team","Account Security","Microsoft 계정")
   or Subject has_any ("account security","security alert","one-time password","OTP","unusual activity","abnormal activity","보안 알림","비정상","암호를 변경")
| where SenderFromDomain !endswith "microsoft.com" and SenderFromDomain !endswith "microsoftonline.com" and SenderFromDomain !endswith "accountprotection.microsoft.com"

    EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderDisplayName, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, FileName, FileType, SHA256, DeliveryAction, AuthenticationDetails
| order by Timestamp desc

NarwhalRAT LNK-spawned batch downloader fetching payload + CAT file from APT37 C2 AIDelivery High
Detects the multi-stage loader where a launched LNK drives cmd/PowerShell/LOLBin downloaders to retrieve the obfuscated batch script, Python binary and Windows security catalog (CAT) file from APT37 C2 hosts. Fires on a download utility whose command line references the named C2 domains or pulls a .cat over HTTP. Rationale: Pins the article's loader stage on the five corroborated C2 domains appearing in a LOLBin command line, plus the distinctive '.cat over HTTP' fetch — both are high-fidelity, low-FP because legitimate software does not download a security catalog from these Korean relay hosts. Cross-checked against: • https://www.genians.co.kr/en/blog/threat_intelligence/narwhalrat • https://cybersecuritynews.com/powershell-and-python-loader-to-deploy-narwhalrat/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal admin script that happens to fetch a legitimately-hosted .cat catalog over HTTP for driver signing
  • Security researcher manually curling one of the C2 domains during analysis on a sandbox/host with telemetry
  • Web-content filter test scripts referencing flagged domains in command lines
  • PowerShell deployment tooling using DownloadFile to a benign internal mirror that an analyst mis-tunes the domain list against
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree — confirm the parent is explorer.exe (LNK launch) or a batch under cmd.exe, and resolve which C2 domain/.cat was fetched. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the five C2 domains at proxy/DNS, and quarantine the downloaded python binary + CAT file. 3) Hunt: check the same host for the scheduled task names (UC3), %APPDATA%\naverwhale (UC4), and outbound C2/pCloud beacons (UC5/UC6); sweep the org for the same parent-LNK pattern.
let LookbackDays = 14d;
let C2Domains = dynamic(["daehoat.com","novel21.co.kr","fe01.co.kr","webhostingkorea.com","crwellfood.com"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (C2Domains)
   or (ProcessCommandLine has ".cat" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","DownloadFile","DownloadString","-urlcache","Start-BitsTransfer","Invoke-WebRequest"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentProcess = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2Domains = dynamic(["daehoat.com","novel21.co.kr","fe01.co.kr","webhostingkorea.com","crwellfood.com"]);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","mshta.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any (C2Domains)
   or (CommandLine has ".cat" and CommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","DownloadFile","-urlcache","Start-BitsTransfer","Invoke-WebRequest"))
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("explorer.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 3b71e2c4-5d18-4f6a-9c0b-1e7a2d9f4c63
status: experimental
description: Detects a Windows command shell or download LOLBin whose command line references APT37/ScarCruft NarwhalRAT C2 domains during the multi-stage LNK loader chain.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/fake-microsoft-alerts-used-to-deploy.html

tags:

logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\certutil.exe'
      - '\bitsadmin.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'daehoat.com'
      - 'novel21.co.kr'
      - 'fe01.co.kr'
      - 'webhostingkorea.com'
      - 'crwellfood.com'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\cmd.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\curl.exe OR *\certutil.exe OR *\bitsadmin.exe OR *\mshta.exe OR *\CMD.EXE OR *\PowerShell.exe) @CommandLine:(*daehoat.com* OR *novel21.co.kr* OR *fe01.co.kr* OR *webhostingkorea.com* OR *crwellfood.com*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/(cmd|powershell|pwsh|curl|certutil|bitsadmin|mshta)\.exe$/i
| ParentBaseFileName=/(explorer|cmd|wscript|cscript|powershell)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/(daehoat\.com|novel21\.co\.kr|fe01\.co\.kr|webhostingkorea\.com|crwellfood\.com)/i
| table([_time, aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","mshta.exe")) (Processes.process="*daehoat.com*" OR Processes.process="*novel21.co.kr*" OR Processes.process="*fe01.co.kr*" OR Processes.process="*webhostingkorea.com*" OR Processes.process="*crwellfood.com*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","mshta.exe")) (Processes.process="*daehoat.com*" OR Processes.process="*novel21.co.kr*" OR Processes.process="*fe01.co.kr*" OR Processes.process="*webhostingkorea.com*" OR Processes.process="*crwellfood.com*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process

NarwhalRAT scheduled-task persistence by exact task name (MicrosoftUserInterfacePicturesUpdateTackMachine) AIInstallation High
Detects creation of the uniquely-named scheduled tasks APT37 uses to persist NarwhalRAT and its sibling Python chain. The names 'MicrosoftUserInterfacePicturesUpdateTackMachine' and 'MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackageTaskMachine' are attacker-specific masquerades and have no legitimate use. Rationale: The two task names are verbatim, attacker-coined strings from the article (note the deliberate 'Tack'/'Task' typo) with zero legitimate footprint — effectively a behavioural hash, making this near-zero-FP alerting. Cross-checked against: • https://www.genians.co.kr/en/blog/threat_intelligence/narwhalrat • https://gbhackers.com/apt37-hackers-use-narwhalrat-malware/
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-hunt or detection-validation exercise that re-creates the named task in a lab
  • Red-team emulation of APT37 reusing the published task name
  • Backup/restore of a previously-compromised system image re-registering the task
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the task's action (schtasks /query /tn <name> /xml) — confirm it launches the CAT/Python in-memory chain, and identify the user context. 2) Contain: delete the task (schtasks /delete), isolate the host, and capture the CAT file + %APPDATA%\naverwhale contents before remediation. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for both task names and for the loader (UC2) and C2 (UC5/UC6); review who received the fake MS alert email (UC1).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("MicrosoftUserInterfacePicturesUpdateTackMachine","MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackageTaskMachine")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (4698, 4688)
| where (EventID == 4698 and (EventData has "MicrosoftUserInterfacePicturesUpdateTackMachine" or EventData has "MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackageTaskMachine"))
   or (EventID == 4688 and NewProcessName endswith "schtasks.exe" and (CommandLine has "MicrosoftUserInterfacePicturesUpdateTackMachine" or CommandLine has "MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackageTaskMachine"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, Account, EventID, NewProcessName, CommandLine, EventData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NarwhalRAT 'naverwhale' staging directory under %APPDATA% AIActions on Objectives High
Detects file activity in the %APPDATA%\naverwhale directory NarwhalRAT uses to stage harvested data (keystrokes, screenshots, audio, USB and directory dumps). The folder name masquerades as Naver Whale browser and is the malware's namesake. Rationale: The literal staging path %APPDATA%\naverwhale is the malware's named artifact (the 'NarwhalRAT' moniker derives from it) and has no legitimate Naver Whale equivalent in Roaming — a single-string, high-confidence host indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://www.genians.co.kr/en/blog/threat_intelligence/narwhalrat • https://gbhackers.com/apt37-hackers-use-narwhalrat-malware/
ATT&CKT1074.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Naver Whale browser writing profile data (its real path is under \AppData\Local\Naver\Naver Whale, not \Roaming\naverwhale — so true overlap is rare)
  • Analyst/IR tooling copying a captured sample's folder onto a telemetry-monitored workstation
  • Backup software indexing a previously-infected user profile
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\Naver\Naver Whale")
Response runbook
1) Triage: enumerate naverwhale folder contents and the InitiatingProcess writing to it (expect python.exe / pythonw.exe), and confirm path is under \Roaming (not the legit \Local\Naver\Naver Whale). 2) Contain: isolate the host, preserve the directory for forensics (it holds staged keystroke/screenshot/audio data), then remove the scheduled task and payload. 3) Hunt: correlate the writing process to outbound C2 (UC5) and pCloud exfil (UC6); scope which data types were staged to gauge exposure.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\AppData\Roaming\naverwhale" or FolderPath has @"\naverwhale\"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\AppData\Roaming\naverwhale" or TargetFilePath has "naverwhale"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NarwhalRAT C2 to APT37 Korean relay domains/IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Detects host connections to the corroborated NarwhalRAT primary C2 relays (daehoat.com, novel21.co.kr and four sibling domains plus six C2 IPs). These Korean-hosted relays are the malware's main command channel per Genians. Rationale: Uses the six C2 IPs and five domains corroborated across Genians/gbhackers; matching them in network/DNS telemetry is a direct IOC hit with negligible FP outside of intentional analyst lookups. Cross-checked against: • https://www.genians.co.kr/en/blog/threat_intelligence/narwhalrat • https://gbhackers.com/apt37-hackers-use-narwhalrat-malware/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC/TI analyst manually browsing or sandbox-detonating against the listed domains from a monitored host
  • Proxy/IDS signature-test traffic deliberately generated to these IOCs
  • Stale IOC: one of the Korean relays gets reclaimed/parked and reused by a benign site (re-validate domains periodically)
  • Threat-intel feed connector pre-fetching the domains for enrichment
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess making the connection (expect python.exe/pythonw.exe staging from %APPDATA%\naverwhale) and the volume/cadence of beacons. 2) Contain: block all five domains and six IPs at perimeter/DNS, isolate any beaconing host. 3) Hunt: pivot from each hitting host to the loader (UC2), scheduled task (UC3) and naverwhale staging (UC4); check for the secondary pCloud dead-drop channel (UC6) in case primary C2 is blocked.
let C2Domains = dynamic(["daehoat.com","novel21.co.kr","fe01.co.kr","webhostingkorea.com","crwellfood.com"]);
let C2IPs = dynamic(["121.254.222.10","121.254.222.80","211.239.157.126","218.150.78.198","218.150.78.231","61.100.9.206"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (C2Domains) or RemoteIP in (C2IPs)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2Domains = dynamic(["daehoat.com","novel21.co.kr","fe01.co.kr","webhostingkorea.com","crwellfood.com"]);
let C2IPs = dynamic(["121.254.222.10","121.254.222.80","211.239.157.126","218.150.78.198","218.150.78.231","61.100.9.206"]);
union
  (DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Name has_any (C2Domains) | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Indicator = Name, Kind = "dns"),
  (ImNetworkSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DstIpAddr in (C2IPs) or Url has_any (C2Domains) | project TimeGenerated, Computer = DvcHostname, ClientIP = SrcIpAddr, Indicator = coalesce(Url, DstIpAddr), Kind = "conn")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NarwhalRAT pCloud dead-drop resolver secondary C2 from Python loader AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the malware's secondary C2 channel: a non-browser Python process reaching pCloud cloud-storage endpoints, used as a dead-drop resolver (the code processes pCloud 'folderid'/'auth' parameters). Correlated to hosts that also show the naverwhale staging directory to cut benign pCloud usage. Rationale: Targets the article's named secondary channel — Python (the NarwhalRAT runtime) abusing the pCloud API as a dead-drop resolver. Host-scoping the Defender/Sentinel variants to machines with the naverwhale artifact suppresses the bulk of legitimate pCloud-client traffic; the EDR variants additionally require python.exe (not the pCloud desktop client) as the initiator. Cross-checked against: • https://www.genians.co.kr/en/blog/threat_intelligence/narwhalrat • https://cybersecuritynews.com/powershell-and-python-loader-to-deploy-narwhalrat/
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate pCloud desktop sync client or browser uploading user files (excluded here by requiring python.exe initiator / naverwhale host)
  • A data-science workstation running python scripts that legitimately call the pCloud API
  • Developer using a pcloud Python SDK for backups
  • CI/automation agent built on Python pushing artifacts to pCloud
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("pcloud.exe","pclouddrive.exe","msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating binary is python.exe/pythonw.exe (not pcloud.exe) and that the host carries %APPDATA%\naverwhale; capture the URL/folderid if visible in proxy logs. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block pcloud.com egress for that asset, and revoke/rotate any credentials that may have been staged. 3) Hunt: tie the Python process back to the scheduled-task chain (UC3) and primary C2 (UC5); review whether exfil to pCloud succeeded by sizing outbound bytes, and sweep other naverwhale hosts for the same pCloud pattern.
let NaverwhaleHosts = DeviceFileEvents

DeviceNetworkEvents

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let NaverwhaleHosts = ImFileEvent

ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "pcloud.com" or DstHostname has "pcloud.com"
| where DvcHostname in (NaverwhaleHosts)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcUsername, SrcIpAddr, Url, DstHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("3715092aa00f380cefe8b4d2eddb7d08", "7cef19f9c4480adac0cd4702ff98f46c", "7eb9cee1f696727752169f25cf79a338", "b6b0602310bb2d4360c52685119aac1b") or SHA1 in~ ("3715092aa00f380cefe8b4d2eddb7d08", "7cef19f9c4480adac0cd4702ff98f46c", "7eb9cee1f696727752169f25cf79a338", "b6b0602310bb2d4360c52685119aac1b") or MD5 in~ ("3715092aa00f380cefe8b4d2eddb7d08", "7cef19f9c4480adac0cd4702ff98f46c", "7eb9cee1f696727752169f25cf79a338", "b6b0602310bb2d4360c52685119aac1b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("3715092aa00f380cefe8b4d2eddb7d08", "7cef19f9c4480adac0cd4702ff98f46c", "7eb9cee1f696727752169f25cf79a338", "b6b0602310bb2d4360c52685119aac1b") or SHA1 in~ ("3715092aa00f380cefe8b4d2eddb7d08", "7cef19f9c4480adac0cd4702ff98f46c", "7eb9cee1f696727752169f25cf79a338", "b6b0602310bb2d4360c52685119aac1b") or MD5 in~ ("3715092aa00f380cefe8b4d2eddb7d08", "7cef19f9c4480adac0cd4702ff98f46c", "7eb9cee1f696727752169f25cf79a338", "b6b0602310bb2d4360c52685119aac1b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["3715092aa00f380cefe8b4d2eddb7d08", "7cef19f9c4480adac0cd4702ff98f46c", "7eb9cee1f696727752169f25cf79a338", "b6b0602310bb2d4360c52685119aac1b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cisco Releases Security Updates for Actively Exploited SD-WAN Manager Flaw

The Hacker News
2026-06-16 7 use cases 2 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cisco has released security updates for a medium-severity security flaw in Catalyst SD-WAN Manager that has come under active exploitation in the wild. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-20262, carries a CVSS score of 6.5 out of 10.0.
