VS Code/Cursor 'runOn folderOpen' tasks.json auto-execution spawning a script interpreter AIExploitation High
Hunts the signature UNK_DeadDrop/Contagious Interview primitive: a cloned 'coding assignment' repo ships a hidden .vscode/tasks.json that abuses VS Code's and Cursor's runOn:folderOpen task automation to execute a loader the instant the folder is opened, with no user interaction. Detects Code.exe / Cursor.exe spawning a script host (wscript/cscript/powershell/bash/sh), which is anomalous for the editor process itself. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit 'runOn folderOpen' technique in .vscode/tasks.json executing on folder open in VS Code/Cursor; the editor process spawning wscript/cscript (the named Windows VBScript loader) is the high-fidelity discriminator. Cross-checked Proofpoint UNK_DeadDrop write-up and CyberSecurityNews. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/dont-fear-repo-unkdeaddrop-phishing-campaign-targets-developers-steal • https://cybersecuritynews.com/north-korea-aligned-hackers-abuse-github-repositories/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.005 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer using the VS Code integrated terminal to launch PowerShell/bash manually
  • A legitimate workspace tasks.json that runs a PowerShell build/lint step on folder open
  • WSL/Git-Bash integrations spawning bash.exe from Code.exe
  • Extension-driven shells (e.g. a test runner that shells out)
  • Cursor AI agent executing an approved terminal command
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has_any ("build","npm run","tsc","eslint","pytest","jest") and Editor == "Code.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full tasks.json from the opened workspace and the child process command line; confirm whether a 'runOn':'folderOpen' task exists and what it executes. Check repo origin (was it git-cloned from an emailed GitHub link in the last 24h?). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the loader and any child wscript/cscript/node tree, and quarantine the cloned repo folder. 3) Hunt: check DeviceNetworkEvents on that host for 23.137.105.75:5173 and the other campaign IPs, look for VSIX sideloads (--install-extension) and browser wallet/credential file reads, and search the org for the same repo URL across mailboxes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("Code.exe","Cursor.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Editor=InitiatingProcessFileName, EditorCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Child=FileName, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("Code.exe","Cursor.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","mshta.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

UNK_DeadDrop Windows loader: VBScript/CMD chain sideloading a named malicious Jupyter VSIX AIInstallation High
Detects the Windows infection chain where a VBScript loader runs a CMD file that installs a malicious VS Code extension (VSIX) masquerading as a Jupyter/Google productivity tool. Keys on the three Yeeth-Security-named extensions and on the 'code --install-extension' sideload of a local .vsix file driven by a script-host parent — a combination that does not occur in benign extension installs from the Marketplace UI. Rationale: Uses the three exact malicious VSIX names from Yeeth Security (ByteBinTools.jupyter-powerdev-2026.6.8, ToolCraft.jupyter-powertools-3.21.0, OLDev.markdown-mode-devtools-2.1.0) plus the local-VSIX sideload pattern (--install-extension <file>.vsix) the loader uses — neither occurs in normal Marketplace installs. Corroborated via The Hacker News reporting on the Yeeth Security findings. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/north-korean-hackers-are-turning.html • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/dont-fear-repo-unkdeaddrop-phishing-campaign-targets-developers-steal
ATT&CKT1059.005 T1059.003 T1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal CI/CD that sideloads pinned internal .vsix files via 'code --install-extension'
  • A developer manually installing a vetted local extension build during testing
  • Air-gapped/offline extension distribution workflows that install VSIX from a share
  • Security team detonation/sandbox of the IOC for analysis
Suppression filter
| where not (ParentCmd has_any ("azure-pipelines","jenkins","\\ci\\","buildagent") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the extension name matches one of the three IOCs or is an unsanctioned local VSIX; enumerate %USERPROFILE%\.vscode\extensions for the publisher folders (ByteBinTools/ToolCraft/OLDev). 2) Contain: uninstall/quarantine the extension folder, isolate the host, and revoke any cloud/dev credentials reachable from that user. 3) Hunt: check for the VBScript/CMD parent chain, outbound to 23.137.105.75:5173, SharePoint/Microsoft Graph API C2 traffic (Graph token use by node.exe), and the same VSIX across other developer endpoints.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("jupyter-powerdev","jupyter-powertools","markdown-mode-devtools","ByteBinTools","ToolCraft.jupyter","OLDev.markdown")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "--install-extension" and ProcessCommandLine has ".vsix")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, Parent=InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has_any ("jupyter-powerdev","jupyter-powertools","markdown-mode-devtools","ByteBinTools","ToolCraft.jupyter","OLDev.markdown")
   or (CommandLine has "--install-extension" and CommandLine has ".vsix")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

UNK_DeadDrop C2 egress to 23.137.105[.]75:5173 and related campaign IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Network IOC detection for the UNK_DeadDrop exfiltration server. The Windows pipeline POSTs harvested ZIPs to 23.137.105[.]75 on TCP/5173 then terminates; Linux/macOS Overlord agents beacon to the same and adjacent infrastructure. Any outbound connection to these confirmed IPs (with 5173 as the documented port) is high-confidence campaign activity. Rationale: Pre-extracted, article-named C2/exfil IPs (23.137.105.75 with the documented POST port 5173, plus 170.205.29.83 and 170.205.30.227). The article explicitly states the Windows pipeline uploads ZIPs to 23.137.105.75:5173. Projecting InitiatingProcess surfaces the responsible binary for triage without a placeholder pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/north-korean-hackers-are-turning.html • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/dont-fear-repo-unkdeaddrop-phishing-campaign-targets-developers-steal
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel feed scanners or honeyclients deliberately touching the IOC IP
  • A security analyst sandbox detonating the sample
  • Shared-hosting IP reuse where a benign service later occupies the same address (validate WHOIS/age)
  • Internal proxy/IDS that mirrors/replays traffic to the IP for inspection
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess and user on the connecting host; confirm whether a recent GitHub repo clone or VSIX install preceded the beacon. 2) Contain: block the three IPs at egress/firewall, isolate the host, and capture the staged ZIP(s) from temp before they are cleaned up. 3) Hunt: pivot on the InitiatingProcess hash org-wide, look for the tasks.json/VBScript loader chain and browser-wallet file reads, and rotate any crypto-wallet/dev credentials accessed from the host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("23.137.105.75","170.205.29.83","170.205.30.227")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("23.137.105.75","170.205.29.83","170.205.30.227")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Contagious Interview Git hooks: .githooks/pre-commit firing a shell on repo clone/commit AIInstallation Medium
Detects the Contagious Interview shift to Git hook execution, where a cloned 'coding assessment' repo carries a .githooks/pre-commit that fires malicious code on first commit/clone. Keys on git.exe spawning a shell/script interpreter whose command line references .githooks or pre-commit — a behaviour distinct from normal IDE-driven git operations. Rationale: Anchored on the article's named persistence/trigger path '.githooks/pre-commit' that Contagious Interview now uses instead of .vscode/tasks.json or package.json. Requiring the .githooks/pre-commit token on the command line keeps it from firing on ordinary git activity. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/north-korean-hackers-are-turning.html
ATT&CKT1546 T1059 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate pre-commit framework (pre-commit.com) running linters/formatters via Python or node
  • Husky git hooks invoking node-based checks in JS projects
  • A monorepo with a custom .githooks directory configured via core.hooksPath
  • Developer running 'git commit' that triggers an approved local hook script
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has_any ("husky","pre-commit.com","lint-staged","prettier","black --","flake8"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the .githooks/pre-commit (and core.hooksPath config) in the repo; determine whether it executes a build/lint tool (benign) or fetches/decodes a payload (malicious). Check repo origin and clone time. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the hook-spawned process tree, and remove/quarantine the repo. 3) Hunt: look for follow-on C2 to the campaign IPs, VSIX sideloads, and the same repo cloned elsewhere; review the developer's own repos for injected commits (worm-like propagation).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","node.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".githooks" or ProcessCommandLine has "pre-commit" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has ".githooks"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Parent=InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Child=FileName, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("git.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","node.exe")
| where CommandLine has ".githooks" or CommandLine has "pre-commit"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Named malicious Jupyter/Markdown VSIX extensions written to the VS Code extensions directory AIInstallation High
File-event detection for the three Yeeth-Security-identified malicious extensions landing in a user's VS Code extensions folder. Catches the install regardless of vector (Marketplace pull or local sideload) by matching the exact publisher.extension folder/file names under .vscode\extensions or .cursor\extensions. Rationale: Directly uses the three exact malicious extension identifiers (ByteBinTools.jupyter-powerdev-2026.6.8, ToolCraft.jupyter-powertools-3.21.0, OLDev.markdown-mode-devtools-2.1.0) from Yeeth Security. These strings are unique to the campaign, giving a very low FP rate. Cross-checked against The Hacker News coverage. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/north-korean-hackers-are-turning.html
ATT&CKT1176 T1505
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security tooling staging the IOC files for analysis/quarantine
  • EDR/AV writing the file to a quarantine path (matches on substring) — validate ActionType and folder
  • Backup software copying a previously-infected profile
  • Threat-hunt team intentionally restoring the sample on a sandbox host
Suppression filter
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified") and FolderPath has_any ("\\.vscode\\extensions","\\.cursor\\extensions")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the FolderPath is a live .vscode/.cursor extensions directory (not a quarantine/backup path) and identify the writing process and user. 2) Contain: remove the extension folder, isolate the host, terminate VS Code/Cursor and any node.exe child handling Graph/SharePoint C2, and revoke the user's M365/Graph tokens. 3) Hunt: search CloudAppEvents/Graph for SharePoint sites used as a command queue, look for the VBScript loader and outbound to 23.137.105.75:5173, and sweep all developer endpoints for the same extension IDs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has_any ("jupyter-powerdev","jupyter-powertools","markdown-mode-devtools","ByteBinTools.jupyter","ToolCraft.jupyter","OLDev.markdown")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("jupyter-powerdev","jupyter-powertools","markdown-mode-devtools","ByteBinTools.jupyter","ToolCraft.jupyter","OLDev.markdown")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

North Korea supply-chain packages: malicious npm/Packagist deps dropped into a project tree AIDelivery Medium
Detects on-disk presence/installation of the named malicious packages tied to the broader North Korean developer-targeting activity: npm redeem-onchain-sdk, nicegui, period-newline (Axios follow-up stealers) and the compromised Packagist package roberts/leads (PHP→JS loader to DEV#POPPER). Matches package directories under node_modules/ or vendor/ created by a package manager. Rationale: Uses the exact malicious package names/versions from the article (redeem-onchain-sdk@1.0.7, nicegui@0.1.4, period-newline@0.1.0, Packagist roberts/leads). Pathing to node_modules/vendor scopes it to actual installation rather than mention. Corroborated by SafeDep's redeem-onchain-sdk analysis and Google/GTIG's Axios UNC1069 attribution. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/redeem-onchain-sdk-polymarket-npm-malware/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/north-korea-threat-actor-targets-axios-npm-package • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/north-korean-hackers-are-turning.html
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer who legitimately depends on a same-named but unrelated package (validate version: malicious are redeem-onchain-sdk@1.0.7, nicegui@0.1.4, period-newline@0.1.0)
  • Offline npm cache/mirror restoring an old lockfile that still references the package
  • Security research clone of the malicious repo for analysis
  • CI artifact cache rehydrating node_modules from a poisoned lockfile
Suppression filter
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the package's package.json/composer.json and check for postinstall/install scripts and the pinned version against the IOC versions; identify which project lockfile pulled it. 2) Contain: remove the package, purge node_modules/vendor and the npm/composer cache, isolate the host, and rotate developer/cloud/crypto credentials reachable from the build. 3) Hunt: search for outbound stealer C2 from node/python, scan other repos/lockfiles in the org for the same dependency names, and review recent commits for injected dependency lines.

| where FolderPath has_any (@"\node_modules\redeem-onchain-sdk", "/node_modules/redeem-onchain-sdk", @"\node_modules\nicegui", "/node_modules/nicegui", @"\node_modules\period-newline", "/node_modules/period-newline", @"\vendor\roberts\leads", "/vendor/roberts/leads")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\node_modules\redeem-onchain-sdk", "/node_modules/redeem-onchain-sdk", @"\node_modules\nicegui", "/node_modules/nicegui", @"\node_modules\period-newline", "/node_modules/period-newline", @"\vendor\roberts\leads", "/vendor/roberts/leads")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Overlord/VSIX stealer staging ZIP exfil to campaign C2 from a developer-tool process AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the credential/wallet-theft payoff stage: a developer-tooling process (node, Code/Cursor, python, or the script-host loader) opening an outbound connection to the campaign C2 — either the named IPs or the documented TCP/5173 to a public host. The article states the Windows pipeline uploads ZIPs of stolen browser-wallet/credential data then terminates, so process-attributed egress complements the pure IOC rule even if infrastructure rotates. Rationale: Combines the article's named C2 IPs and the explicit exfil port (5173) with the developer-tooling process set that performs the theft (node/Code/python/script-host), targeting the stated 'upload ZIPs then terminate' behaviour. Process attribution keeps signal if the IP rotates while public-only gating on 5173 avoids local Vite dev-server noise. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/north-korean-hackers-are-turning.html • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/dont-fear-repo-unkdeaddrop-phishing-campaign-targets-developers-steal
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1041 T1005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A local front-end dev server (Vite defaults to TCP/5173) reached over the internet via a tunnel/proxy — gate kept to public IPs reduces but won't eliminate
  • node/python build tooling legitimately POSTing telemetry to a 5173 cloud endpoint
  • A self-hosted internal service that happens to listen on 5173 behind a public IP
  • Security sandbox replaying the sample's C2
Suppression filter
| where not (RemotePort == 5173 and RemoteUrl has_any ("localhost","127.0.0.1"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process command line and whether stolen-data ZIPs were staged in temp/AppData before the connection; confirm the destination is not an internal/dev Vite server. 2) Contain: block the destination, isolate the host, and immediately rotate all browser-stored credentials and crypto-wallet seed/keys for the user. 3) Hunt: pull DeviceFileEvents for .zip writes by the same process and reads of browser 'Local Extension Settings'/wallet app data, then sweep for the loader chain and VSIX IOCs across other developer endpoints.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","Code.exe","Cursor.exe","python.exe","pythonw.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where RemoteIP in ("23.137.105.75","170.205.29.83","170.205.30.227")
   or (RemotePort == 5173 and RemoteIPType == "Public")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("23.137.105.75","170.205.29.83","170.205.30.227")
   or (DstPortNumber == 5173 and not(ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr)))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"

          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

SecurityEvent

status: experimental
description: |

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/

            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0b
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__HASH_LIST__` placeholder with article-specific SHA256
    values. Use a watchlist or external indicator file for management
    at scale.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    category: process_creation

            - 'SHA256=__HASH_PLACEHOLDER_REPLACE_ME__'

level: critical

Critical

LiteLLM Vulnerability Chain Lets Low-Privilege Users Take Over AI Gateway Servers

The Hacker News
2026-06-15 4 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A default low-privilege account on a LiteLLM proxy can climb to full admin and run code on the server by chaining three vulnerabilities, researchers at Obsidian Security disclosed LiteLLM is a widely deployed open-source AI gateway that brokers calls to more than 100 model providers behind one OpenAI-compatible interface. A server takeover exposes every provider key it holds, the secrets that

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:

    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser

Microsoft Defender email security benchmarking: Key insights from one year of data

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-06-15 5 use cases 3 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

See how Microsoft Defender performed in one year of real-world email security benchmarking against SEG and ICES vendors. The post Microsoft Defender email security benchmarking: Key insights from one year of data appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

ATT&CKT1195.002 T1566 T1566.001

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] EvilTokens device-code token polling from attacker infra (python-requests UA / C2 IPs) · [LLM] EvilTokens device-code lure email (Acrobat/DocuSign decoy, 'Verify to view') · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Microsoft 365 OAuth device code authentication flow sign-in (EvilTokens) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains

Microsoft 365 OAuth device code authentication flow sign-in (EvilTokens) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces successful Entra ID sign-ins that completed via the OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant flow — the exact mechanism EvilTokens abuses to have a victim authorize the attacker's session on the genuine microsoft.com/devicelogin page. In tenants that don't legitimately use device code flow, any occurrence is a strong account-takeover indicator. Rationale: Anchors on the OAuth device code grant — the single behaviour that defines EvilTokens — surfaced via the AuthenticationProcessingDetails 'Device Code' marker (Defender/Sentinel) and AuthenticationProtocol=deviceCode (Sigma). Microsoft and Sekoia both confirm deviceCode/originalTransferMethod fields are the primary detection surface and are absent from normal interactive sign-ins. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/ • https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-oauth-device-code-phishing-m365-20260325-c/
ATT&CKT1528 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running 'az login --use-device-code' from a workstation
  • Sysadmin connecting Microsoft Graph PowerShell with -UseDeviceAuthentication
  • Conference-room / smart-TV / kiosk device enrollment using device code
  • Legacy line-of-business app onboarded via device code grant
  • Help-desk provisioning a shared device on behalf of a user
Suppression filter
| where tostring(parse_json(tostring(DeviceDetail)).trustType) !in ("Azure AD joined", "Hybrid Azure AD joined")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the sign-in's IPAddress, UserAgent, AppDisplayName and DeviceTrust. Managed/compliant device + corporate IP + Azure CLI/PowerShell app = likely admin self-service; unmanaged device + VPS/residential-proxy IP + python-requests UA = treat as compromise. 2) Contain: if suspicious, revoke the user's sessions and refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), force password reset, and require re-MFA. 3) Hunt: review the same user's subsequent mailbox access, new inbox rules, OneDrive/SharePoint downloads, and any Teams/Graph activity from the same IP in the following 72h.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails contains "Device Code"
| where AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, City, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, RiskState
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails contains "Device Code"
| extend DeviceTrust = tostring(parse_json(tostring(DeviceDetail)).trustType)
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, Location, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed, DeviceTrust, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, RiskState
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EvilTokens device-code token polling from attacker infra (python-requests UA / C2 IPs) AIDelivery Medium
Detects device-code sign-ins originating from the EvilTokens C2 IP ranges or carrying the python-requests user-agent characteristic of the kit's token-polling loop against Microsoft's devicecode endpoint. This is the attacker's authenticating 'device' picking up access/refresh tokens after the victim enters the code. Rationale: Combines the corroborated device-code protocol with two high-fidelity discriminators: the python-requests token-polling user-agent (named in Microsoft's Storm-2372 analysis) and the article's EvilTokens IP ranges (treated as /24 from the .0 IOCs). The TTP+UA pair is cross-confirmed; the specific IPs are article-sourced enrichment. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1078.004 T1528
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal Python automation/script using device code flow against Graph (uncommon)
  • Security scanner or red-team tooling emulating device code phishing
  • Shared NAT egress where a single corporate IP overlaps a flagged hosting range (unlikely for the listed VPS blocks)
  • Pen-test of conditional access device-code policy
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the AccountUpn, the AppDisplayName the token was minted for, and whether the source IP is a known VPS/hosting block; python-requests + device code is effectively never benign for end-user accounts. 2) Contain: immediately revoke sessions and refresh tokens for the account, disable the account if active mailbox/Graph access is seen, and add the IP ranges to a block/Conditional-Access named location. 3) Hunt: sweep all other accounts that authenticated from the same IPs in the last 30 days, and pivot to OfficeActivity/CloudAppEvents for inbox-rule creation and mass downloads.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails contains "Device Code"
| where UserAgent has "python-requests"
    or ipv4_is_in_any_range(IPAddress, "162.220.232.0/24", "162.220.234.0/24", "89.150.45.0/24", "185.81.113.0/24")
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, City, UserAgent, ErrorCode, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, RiskState
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails contains "Device Code"
| where UserAgent has "python-requests"
    or ipv4_is_in_any_range(IPAddress, "162.220.232.0/24", "162.220.234.0/24", "89.150.45.0/24", "185.81.113.0/24")
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, Location, UserAgent, ResultType, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, RiskState
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EvilTokens device-code lure email (Acrobat/DocuSign decoy, 'Verify to view') AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound mail delivering the EvilTokens lure — links to the kit's decoy domains or subjects impersonating document/signature/calendar requests that route the victim toward microsoft.com/devicelogin. Targets the delivery step before the victim ever enters the attacker's code. Rationale: Pivots on the kit's named decoy domains (authdocspro/docusend impersonating DocuSign, eventcalender-schedule for the calendar-invite lure) plus the article's verbatim lure strings 'Verify to view' / 'Signature required', combined with a devicelogin URL target. Domains are article-sourced; the Acrobat/DocuSign decoy theme is corroborated by Sekoia. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/ • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/cybercrime/eviltokens-phishing-doesnt-steal-password/
ATT&CKT1566.002
Data sourcesEmail
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine DocuSign/Adobe Acrobat Sign notification with a 'Signature required' subject
  • Legitimate SharePoint/OneDrive 'shared a document' invite
  • Internal calendar-invite tooling using 'Verify to access' language
  • Marketing/e-sign vendor newsletters that happen to contain the lure phrasing
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the sending domain's SPF/DKIM/DMARC and the UrlDomain reputation; a freshly-registered look-alike (authdocspro, docusend.networkssolutionmail) routing to devicelogin is high-confidence phishing. 2) Contain: ZAP/soft-delete the message across all recipients, block the sender + URL domains at the secure email gateway, and warn recipients not to enter any code. 3) Hunt: check UrlClickEvents for recipients who clicked, then correlate to SigninLogs for any device-code sign-in by those users within 15 minutes (the code's validity window).
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| join kind=inner (EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain) on NetworkMessageId
| where UrlDomain in~ ("authdocspro.com", "docusend.networkssolutionmail.com", "notificationsmanagersec.com", "eventcalender-schedule.com", "newmobilepolojean.com", "evobothub.org", "framebound.cloud", "infinitechai.org", "backdoor-hub.com")
    or (Subject has_any ("Verify to view", "Signature required", "Signature requested", "Verify to access") and Url has "devicelogin")
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderDisplayName, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url, UrlDomain, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"

Post-device-code malicious inbox rule creation (BEC prep) AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates a recent device-code sign-in by a user with that same user creating an auto-delete/forward/move inbox rule — the EvilTokens post-compromise pattern where attackers hide replies and stage BEC. Ties two telemetry sources to cut the noise of routine rule changes. Rationale: Gates the well-known malicious-inbox-rule signal behind a recent device-code sign-in by the same identity, making it specific to the EvilTokens account-takeover chain rather than a generic rule-change hunt. The hide/forward parameter keywords match the article's 'new inbox rules' warning and corroborated BEC staging behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/ • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/cybercrime/eviltokens-phishing-doesnt-steal-password/
ATT&CKT1564.008 T1114.003
Data sourcesChange
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User who legitimately enrolled a device via device code then set up a normal folder-organization rule
  • Admin/help-desk creating delegate or archive rules on a mailbox
  • Outlook 'sweep'/clutter rule auto-moving newsletters to a folder
  • Legitimate auto-forward to a personal-archive mailbox approved by policy
Suppression filter
| where not (Parameters has "MoveToFolder" and Parameters !has_any ("ForwardTo", "RedirectTo", "DeleteMessage", "Deleted Items", "RSS Feeds"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the rule's Parameters/RawEventData — forwarding to an external address or moving replies to RSS Feeds/Deleted Items/Archive is hostile; benign rules sort known senders into named folders. 2) Contain: delete the malicious inbox rule, revoke the user's sessions/refresh tokens, reset credentials, and disable external auto-forwarding tenant-wide if not required. 3) Hunt: review Sent Items and OfficeActivity for outbound BEC messages, check whether finance/HR/AP counterparties were contacted, and pivot on the sign-in IP to find other compromised mailboxes.
let DeviceCodeUsers = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where ErrorCode == 0
    | where AuthenticationProcessingDetails contains "Device Code"
    | distinct AccountObjectId;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in~ ("New-InboxRule", "Set-InboxRule", "UpdateInboxRules")
| where AccountObjectId in (DeviceCodeUsers)
| where tostring(RawEventData) has_any ("DeleteMessage", "MoveToFolder", "ForwardTo", "RedirectTo", "Deleted Items", "Junk Email", "RSS Feeds", "Archive", "MarkAsRead")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, ActionType, ObjectName, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
let DeviceCodeUsers = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where ResultType == 0
    | where AuthenticationProcessingDetails contains "Device Code"
    | distinct UserPrincipalName;
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Operation in~ ("New-InboxRule", "Set-InboxRule", "UpdateInboxRules")
| where UserId in~ (DeviceCodeUsers)
| where Parameters has_any ("DeleteMessage", "MoveToFolder", "ForwardTo", "RedirectTo", "Deleted Items", "Junk Email", "RSS Feeds", "Archive", "MarkAsRead")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, ClientIP, Operation, Parameters, OriginatingServer
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,

let BadIPs     = dynamic(["162.220.232.0", "162.220.234.0", "89.150.45.0", "185.81.113.0"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["authdocspro.com", "backdoor-hub.com", "bumpgames.net", "carbatterygurgaon.com", "careldutoit-el.co.za", "dao.com.au", "docusend.networkssolutionmail.com", "eqfit.co.za", "eventcalender-schedule.com", "evobothub.org"]);

—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
